title: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA's 0.8% forecast
body: The Australian dollar and front-end yields are set up for a binary reaction. With implied hike odds already above half, a trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would push November pricing closer to fully priced and support the currency. A 0.9% or lower print could see that pricing unwind quickly. Oil is central to the headline story: the fuel spike reflects the global energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would keep headline inflation elevated into year-end. The services component matters most for the RBA, since broadening price pressure would undercut the argument that this is purely an imported energy shock. The release coincides with RBA officials appearing before Senate Estimates, adding to the event risk. --- Earlier: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls --- Australia's core inflation is set to overshoot the RBA's own forecast for another quarter, and with the banks split down the middle, Wednesday's print may decide whether the Board hikes on Melbourne Cup Day.

title: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls
body: For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials' data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff's downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read. --- Yesterday: RBA's Hunter says inflation job not done after four hikes, November rise in view --- The RBA has never been chattier, but Westpac's Luci Ellis says traders hunting for promises should listen instead to how it reads the data, because that is where the real signal lives.

body: There is a bit of a welcome relief in global bonds to start the new week, particularly in Europe after Moody's affirmed France's Aa3 credit rating. Meanwhile, Treasury yields have also settled down a fair bit after an extremely volatile period earlier this month. But in looking at where things are right now, there is still plenty of tension lurking beneath the surface. For one, 10-year Treasury yields are still sitting just below the 5% mark for the time being. And over in Europe, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread remains at levels that would have surely been alarming just a few months ago. So while the selling pressure in the bond market has eased for now, the underlying concerns haven't really changed all that much. And as much as that offers some breathing room for broader markets, there are still plenty of reasons to be cautious. The Fed decision tomorrow is one obvious catalyst, even if policymakers are widely expected to leave interst rates unchanged. And beyond that, I'm also keeping a close watch on big tech earnings this week. On the latter, there's a growing concern over whether the enormous spending behind the AI boom can actually justify the returns. And if earnings from the likes of Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all back that sentiment, we could see a rather nasty bout of volatility kick in again. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Why the Federal Reserve matters more to crypto market than many investors realise
body: Cryptocurrencies have different use cases and fundamentals, but the macroeconomic conditions are an important underlying driver. The Federal Reserve's policy has an enormous influence on macroeconomic conditions through liquidity, borrowing costs and risk appetite, making it a key factor for the crypto market. Because cryptocurrencies are risk assets, they tend to struggle when monetary policy tightens and benefit when policy becomes more accommodative. By raising interest rates, the Fed increases borrowing costs for households and businesses, restraining consumption and investment. This can slow economic growth and tighten financial conditions. Conversely, rate cuts reduce borrowing costs and can support economic activity by encouraging spending and investment. When growth is resilient and financial conditions are supportive, investors are generally more willing to allocate capital to riskier assets, including cryptocurrencies. During tightening cycles, higher borrowing costs and reduced risk appetite can trigger capital outflows from speculative assets, contributing to corrections or bear markets. During easing cycles, improving liquidity and a greater appetite for risk can support crypto rallies. This helps explain why Bitcoin, Ethereum and many altcoins often move in the same direction during major market swings, even when their underlying fundamentals differ.

title: ECB rate outlook grows more complicated as bank lending conditions tighten
body: The ECB just released its latest bank lending survey and it's not exactly painting a particularly encouraging picture for the euro area economy. Of note, banks are tightening their lending standards further while demand for loans is falling across the board, largely due to the backdrop of higher interest rates continuing to weigh on borrowing activity. According to the October survey, which covers developments in Q3, the main takeaways are: Corporate lending: A net 9% of banks reported tighter credit standards, exceeding the 5% previously expected Consumer credit: A net 14% of banks reported tighter lending standards, while housing loan standards were unchanged Corporate loan demand: Fell by a net 6%, reversing a 3% increase in Q2 Housing loan demand: Slumped by a net 27%, compared with a 15% decline in Q2 In looking to Q4, banks also expected further tightening in lending standards and even weaker household loan demand. So, that's not a good sign of things to come. In any case, the numbers reinforce the message that higher interest rates are already doing their job in slowing the economy. Softer borrowing and tighter credit conditions should eventually weigh on investment, consumption and broader economic activity as a whole. And with banks also needing to navigate through geopolitical uncertainty and worsening risk perceptions, there is little reason to expect credit conditions to improve in the near-term.

title: France consumer confidence plunges to lowest since 2013 as fiscal worries deepen
body: France October consumer confidence 80 vs 85 expected Prior 86; revised to 85 That's a major blow. French household confidence falls to its lowest since 2013 in October as fiscal worries and concerns over the country's public finances weigh heavily on sentiment. That is not a good look as the index strays further away from the long-term average of 100, in which we haven't seen since December 2021. There were marked deteriorations in sentiment among most sub-indices, as households noted worsening past and expected financial situations. Meanwhile, the sub-index measuring past and future standard of living conditions also showed a big drop in October. Adding to those concerns, consumers are also fearing that inflation pressures are going to worsen in the months ahead. The sub-index measuring futures prices rose further to -7 points, its highest since May, and is well off the -32 points recorded in July. Besides that, unemployment fears also picked up with the sub-index there rising by another 5 points to 61 points on the month. That marks the highest level since March 2021. It's an all-round poor report as it signals that the French consumer climate has deterioriated markedly amid the social unrest and fiscal woes. And we're already starting to see that show up in economic data too, with French PMI figures this month already being rather disappointing.

title: China tech stocks plunge as AI trade cracks deepen, is Wall Street next?

And considering how nervous investors have been about the AI trade lately, this may be something worth noting just in case it begins to reverberate across the globe. The CSI Semiconductor Industry index tumbled by nearly 6% today, falling to its lowest level since April. Meanwhile, the CSI Artificial Intelligence index fell by almost 4%, threatening to break below its April lows in a drop to its weakest level since November 2025. Both charts tell a similar story. The semiconductor index has now nearly erased its entire rally since April, while the AI index is struggling to hold at the key support region just below 5,000. A firm break below that could invite another wave of selling. And quite frankly, these aren't exactly small corrections anymore. China's STAR50 index, which includes major AI and semiconductor firms, has already lost roughly 40% in less than four months. That's around $480 billion in market value wiped out as investors are caught in the middle of rethinking lofty valuations and the sustainability of AI demand. The question now is, should Wall Street be worried?

title: Why spreads matter more than you think, Elev8 broker explains
body: The spread, the difference between the bid (selling price) and ask (buying price)—can become a substantial expense when trades are frequent. According to the World Gold Council, average spot-market spreads were 0.02% for gold (XAUUSD) and 0.09% for silver (XAGUSD) between February 2025 and February 2026. It means your choice of instrument can multiply your spread costs: for the same trade value, spreads on silver were 4.5 times higher than on gold. Spreads are also essential for traders who use Contracts for Difference (CFD) as their main instrument. Elev8, a global CFD broker, explains how spreads work, how repeated transactions can turn small price differences into measurable trading costs, and why those costs matter in financial markets. What costs does a trader pay on every trade? Trading costs fall into four main categories: spreads, commissions, swaps, and taxes. Slippage is another potential cost factor, but because it is unpredictable and irregular, it will not be covered in this article. The spread is built into the buying and selling prices, while the other costs depend on the account, holding period, and applicable tax rules. A spread creates a cost even when a trade has no separate commission. What are spreads in trading? The spread is the difference between the ask (the price you buy at) and the bid (the price you sell at). Unlike a separate commission, the spread is built into the quoted prices.

title: US August Case-Shiller 20-city house price index +2.7% y/y vs +2.6% expected
body: Prior was +2.5% y/y 20-city house price index +0.3% m/m vs +0.3% expected Mortgage rates at 7.5% aren't doing any favors for the housing market. For background, the S&P Case-Shiller Home Price Indices are the best-known measure of US house prices. They're published on the last Tuesday of each month at 9 am ET and carry a roughly two-month lag, so a release in late October covers August. The indexes use a repeat-sales method, tracking price changes on the same single-family homes as they sell over time. Because they compare a property with itself, they avoid the distortions that come from changes in the mix of homes being sold, a weakness of simple median price measures. Each monthly reading is a three-month moving average, which smooths the data but adds to the lag. The headline figure is usually the year-over-year change in the 20-city composite index. S&P also publishes a 10-city composite and a national index, along with results for each of the 20 metro areas, which often show sharp regional divergence. Markets focus on the unadjusted annual changes, though seasonally adjusted monthly figures are available. The Federal Housing Finance Agency releases its own house price index at the same time. It covers homes financed with conforming mortgages backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and tends to tell a similar story. The long lag means Case-Shiller rarely moves markets, and by the time it's released, mortgage rates and housing activity may already have shifted.

title: Another Apple launch is off to a bad start
body: It's starting to feel like Apple's tradition: every big launch comes with a problem. The iPhone 4 had signal issues when held a certain way, the iPhone 6 Plus was bending in people's pockets, and the iPhone 15 Pro was getting unusually hot until an iOS update helped fix it. Now it's the iPhone Duo's turn. Just hours after sales kicked off, reports of screens cracking along the fold started coming in, though Apple says only a small number of devices are affected and has advised customers to contact AppleCare for a replacement. Apple shares slipped around 1% on the news, not a huge move, but could this turn into a bigger problem? In similar cases, Apple shares have typically dipped 3–5% over a few days, without driving customers away. Most users have stayed loyal, waiting for fixes rather than switching brands, while Wall Street has quickly moved on, knowing Apple has plenty of cash to cover repairs and legal costs. It's also worth noting that the iPhone Duo was never expected to be a game-changer for Apple's revenue. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, expects Apple to sell 20 million units in fiscal 2027, accounting for roughly 7% of total iPhone sales that year. But there's another risk that could hit Apple: AI.

Warsh is expected to reiterate that monetary policy is not sufficiently restrictive and that additional tightening is warranted. body: Oil is the key driver here: Standard Chartered's warning ties gold's next move directly to crude, with each leg higher in oil feeding inflation and Fed hike expectations, a pressure gold has struggled to withstand. With a December hike largely priced, any hawkish tone from the Fed on Wednesday could push gold toward the $3,886 support. A break there could trigger further liquidation from underwater ETP holders. On the other side, positioning is at its lightest since May and short covering has started, which leaves room for a sharp rebound if oil eases or the dollar softens. Physical buying around Diwali is a near-term test of whether Asian demand can step in where Western investors have pulled back. - Standard Chartered still sees gold higher by early next year, but says it first needs to find a floor while rising oil keeps the Fed in hiking mode. Summary: Standard Chartered says gold must hold $3,886 support after falling below $4,000, warning that a sustained break could bring a much deeper correction. Higher oil prices are keeping inflation risks and Fed tightening expectations in focus. Markets price under a 10% chance of a hike this week and around 86% odds in December. title: AUDUSD trades up and down in a 35 pip trading range over the last 3 days. Look for a break?
body: The AUDUSD has spent the last three trading days moving up and down inside a narrow range, with a low near 0.7005 and a high at 0.70397. That is only about 35 pips from bottom to top. There has been plenty of movement within that range, but limited progress for either the buyers or the sellers. In the video above, I take a look at the technical levels defining that battle and explain why traders should be preparing for a potential break and run. The moving averages tell the story of indecision Inside the range sit two key technical levels: the 100-hour moving average near 0.7023 and the 100-day moving average at 0.70317. The price has been trading above and below those moving averages. A move above has not generated enough buying momentum to get away. A move below has not led to a sustained push lower either. That back-and-forth price action tells us that neither side has been able to take firm control. Moving averages can be useful barometers for the trading bias. However, when the price repeatedly crosses them in a narrow range, traders need to recognize what the market is saying: the directional conviction is limited, and the market is waiting for a catalyst. That catalyst could come from economic data, central bank commentary, or a broader shift in the USD or risk sentiment. The technical chart does not tell us which headline will do it. It does give us levels to judge whether the reaction is changing the picture. What would give the buyers more control?

title: Macro takeaways from earnings: Travel, package delivery and home appliances in focus
body: The US economy is sending some wildly contradictory signals, but four earnings calls this today help to make sense of what's happening beneath the surface. Whirlpool is struggling with weak consumer demand and says Americans are putting off appliance purchases. Royal Caribbean is seeing record cruise bookings at higher prices. Hilton says business travel is booming as the AI and infrastructure investment cycle accelerates, while UPS is seeing explosive growth in high-tech shipments but a mixed picture elsewhere. At first glance, those are four very different stories. Taken together, they paint a picture of an economy that's still growing, but increasingly divided between asset owners and everyone else, with a powerful capital spending boom providing an additional engine of growth. Perhaps the most revealing comment came from UPS CEO Carol Tomé: "It's a bit of a K curve for sure. If you have assets, you're spending. If you don't, you're stretched." That might be the best summary of the US consumer right now. The consumer is still spending, but not on everything Whirlpool expects North American appliance industry demand to decline around 5% this year, with the company describing persistent weakness in discretionary purchases. CEO Marc Bitzer said consumers are increasingly focused on replacing appliances only when they have to, and even some replacement decisions are being delayed.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly flees Brazil for the US after election loss
body: Flávio Bolsonaro is reportedly en route to the United States, according to allies cited by Folha de S.Paulo. That comes just two days after he lost the presidential runoff to Lula, and after the Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports amid criminal investigations. Brazilian authorities then cancelled his Brazilian passport. Allies say he went out through Argentina. Nothing about the route or his current location has been confirmed, so treat this with some caution until there's an official word. If it's accurate, this goes well beyond a losing candidate leaving the country. A presidential runner-up under investigation, travelling without a valid passport, would be landing in a country whose president openly backed him. The family already has a foothold there. His brother Eduardo told Reuters he has received permanent US residency, and has lived in the US since February 2025. Flávio met Trump in the Oval Office back in May. Brasília also denied visas to two US diplomats this summer after spotting a possible link between Flávio's attacks on the voting machines and the Trump administration. So the setup is a likely extradition fight, Washington possibly treating him as a political exile, and a US-Brazil relationship that was already strained heading toward an ugly patch right as Lula starts a new term. It's almost certain that Trump would grant him asylum but it might be more tricky in a subsequent administration.
